practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of quantitative data collected by a retail business?
A) A customer review praising the store layout
B) Staff feedback about the new uniform policy
C) The number of customers who visited the store each day last week
D) A manager's opinion about which products should be promoted
practice_questions.marks: C) The number of customers who visited the store each day last week [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two types of data that a retail business might collect to monitor its performance.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: sales revenue/turnover / footfall / stock/inventory data / customer/loyalty data / profit data. Vague answers such as "information about customers" without naming the type score 0. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a retail manager would choose a line graph rather than a bar chart to display sales revenue data for the past 12 months.
practice_questions.marks: A basic point scores 1 mark (e.g. "a line graph shows change over time"). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. "a line graph connects data points month by month so the manager can clearly see whether sales revenue is rising, falling or remaining stable across the year"). A further developed explanation or contrast with the bar chart scores 3 marks (e.g. add "a bar chart is better for comparing separate categories such as different stores, but it does not show the direction of trend as clearly as a connected line"). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A fashion retailer notices from its sales data that revenue has fallen by 18% over the past three months. Describe how the retailer could use qualitative data to help understand the reason for this fall.
practice_questions.marks:
Description of qualitative data method (up to 2 marks): the retailer could carry out customer surveys or focus groups asking shoppers why they have stopped buying — e.g. the new season range does not appeal to them, prices are too high, or a competitor is offering a better deal (2 marks for a clear, developed description of a method and what it would reveal; 1 mark for naming a qualitative method without explaining how it helps).
Application to the scenario (up to 2 marks): the qualitative data would give the retailer the reason behind the 18% drop which the sales figures alone cannot provide, allowing a targeted solution — e.g. if customers say sizing is the issue, the retailer adjusts the range; if price is the concern, a promotional discount is launched (2 marks for a well-applied explanation linked to the scenario; 1 mark for a general statement). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A supermarket chain provides the following data for four of its stores last month:

Store A — Footfall: 32,000 / Sales revenue: £480,000
Store B — Footfall: 28,000 / Sales revenue: £560,000
Store C — Footfall: 41,000 / Sales revenue: £390,000
Store D — Footfall: 19,000 / Sales revenue: £285,000

Using this data, discuss what the figures suggest about the performance of each store and which store the manager should investigate first.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A discussion that goes beyond simply reading off figures. Notes that Store B has the highest revenue despite lower footfall than Store A or C, suggesting high average spend per customer or an effective product mix; Store C has the highest footfall but the lowest revenue per visitor, suggesting customers are browsing but not buying, which could indicate a pricing, product range or layout problem. Store D has both low footfall and low revenue, which may reflect location or promotion issues. Recommends Store C for priority investigation as it wastes the most traffic. Acknowledges limits of the data (no cost/profit figures available).
Secure (3-4 marks): At least two stores compared with figures quoted and some inference drawn.
Developing (2 marks): Relevant observations but largely descriptive, data quoted without interpretation.
Emerging (1 mark): One relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A national clothing retailer wants to present data showing (a) how its total sales revenue is split between menswear, womenswear and childrenswear, and (b) how overall store footfall has changed month by month over the past year.

Evaluate which data presentation formats would be most appropriate for each purpose and explain why other formats would be less suitable.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): For (a), identifies a pie chart as most suitable because it shows proportions of a whole — the three segments immediately communicate which division accounts for the largest share of total revenue. Notes that a bar chart could work but does not show proportional relationships as clearly; a line graph is unsuitable as there is no time dimension. For (b), identifies a line graph as most suitable because it shows trends over time — the 12 monthly data points connected by a line reveal whether footfall is rising, falling or seasonal. Notes that a bar chart could show the same values but the trend would be less immediately obvious; a pie chart is wholly unsuitable as there is no single total to divide. Evaluative conclusion: the choice of format should match the purpose — proportional data needs a pie chart; time-series data needs a line graph. A single infographic combining both could serve a board presentation.
Secure (5-6 marks): Correct format chosen for each with explanation; some comparison with alternatives.
Developing (3-4 marks): Correct formats identified but justification limited; alternatives not addressed.
Emerging (1-2 marks): One format named with little or no explanation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes direct competition in retail?
A) A cinema and a restaurant competing for the same family's leisure spending
B) Two supermarkets on the same street both selling groceries
C) An online retailer and a physical store competing for different customer groups
D) A department store and a specialist electrical retailer competing for different products
practice_questions.marks: B) Two supermarkets on the same street both selling groceries [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two ways in which a retailer can compete with its rivals other than by lowering its prices.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: quality of products and range / customer service / advertising and promotional activities / store design/layout / location / loyalty schemes. Accept reasonable equivalent phrasing. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by a unique selling point (USP) and why it is important to a retail business.
practice_questions.marks:
Definition (1 mark): a USP is the distinctive feature that makes a retailer's offer different from and more attractive than rivals.
Importance developed (up to 2 marks): it gives customers a clear reason to choose that retailer over alternatives (1 mark); when the USP is hard for rivals to copy it creates a sustainable competitive advantage, helping the retailer retain customers and protect its market share long-term (2 marks for developed explanation). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A national supermarket has annual sales revenue of £4.8 billion. The total UK grocery market is worth £200 billion per year.

Calculate the supermarket's market share. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Working (1 mark): 4.8 ÷ 200 × 100
Answer (1 mark): 2.4%
A second part may be asked: if the supermarket's sales grow to £6 billion next year while the total market stays at £200 billion, what is the new market share? (6 ÷ 200 × 100 = 3%) [1 mark each step shown + correct answer; max 2 marks per calculation; 4 marks total if two-part question]

practice_questions.text:
FreshGrocer is a medium-sized supermarket chain facing growing competition from two large discount rivals that have recently opened stores nearby. FreshGrocer has always competed on price, but its profits are falling.

Discuss two ways FreshGrocer could compete more effectively with its rivals.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Two competitive methods identified and developed with clear reference to the scenario. For example: improving customer service — FreshGrocer could invest in staff training so advisers help shoppers find products and resolve complaints quickly; discount rivals typically cut service costs to keep prices low, so superior service is a differentiation strategy the discounters cannot easily match without raising their own costs (developed point applied to scenario). Loyalty scheme — a points card rewards repeat purchase and generates customer data allowing FreshGrocer to personalise promotions; this creates switching costs that make it harder for customers to move to a rival even if prices are slightly higher (second developed point). Both methods linked to the aim of retaining customers profitably.
Secure (3-4 marks): Two methods identified with some development but limited scenario application.
Developing (2 marks): One method identified and briefly explained.
Emerging (1 mark): A method named with no explanation. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
"Competition in the retail market is good for customers but bad for retail businesses."

Evaluate this statement, using examples to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation covering both sides. Benefits for customers: lower prices as retailers undercut rivals; greater product choice; higher service standards; loyalty scheme rewards; faster innovation (e.g. Aldi/Lidl forcing major supermarkets to improve value ranges). Drawbacks for businesses: margin pressure from price competition; cost of loyalty-scheme infrastructure; need for continuous investment in service, branding and technology just to maintain market share. Substantiated judgement: competition is broadly positive for customers and for the economy, but well-run retailers can still thrive by developing strong USPs and competitive advantages that reduce the pressure of direct price competition — the statement oversimplifies by treating all retailers equally.
Secure (5-6 marks): Both sides covered, some examples, attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Largely one-sided with limited examples.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points, no balance or judgement. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes wholesale?
A) Selling goods directly to members of the public
B) Selling goods in bulk to other businesses
C) Selling goods through an online marketplace
D) Selling goods at a market stall
practice_questions.marks: B) Selling goods in bulk to other businesses [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two retail channels that a clothing retailer could use to sell its products.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct answers from: physical store/bricks-and-mortar / e-commerce / m-commerce / click-and-collect / mail order/catalogue / concession / pop-up shop / market stall. Answers that describe the same channel in different words score only 1 mark. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of using e-commerce as a retail channel.
practice_questions.marks: Advantage (up to 2 marks): e.g. "E-commerce allows the retailer to trade 24 hours a day without the cost of physical premises, reaching customers nationally or globally" — 1 mark for stating an advantage; 2 marks for a developed explanation. Disadvantage (up to 2 marks): e.g. "Customers cannot physically see or try the product before buying, which leads to higher return rates and increased logistics costs" — 1 mark for stating a disadvantage; 2 marks for a developed explanation. [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between a supermarket and a convenience store.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks. Supermarket: large store selling primarily food and grocery products, with a wide range of product lines, typically at competitive prices (1 mark). Convenience store: smaller shop open long hours, selling everyday essentials, valued for accessibility rather than range or price (1 mark). Clear comparison or contrast between the two (1 mark, e.g. noting the difference in size, product range, location or opening hours). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A small independent bakery currently sells only through its one high-street shop. The owner is considering adding an e-commerce channel and a click-and-collect service.

Discuss the likely benefits and drawbacks of this decision for the bakery owner.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion covering multiple benefits (extended customer reach beyond the local area; ability to trade outside shop hours; click-and-collect reduces delivery complexity for a perishable product) and drawbacks (cost of building and maintaining a website; managing online orders alongside in-store trade; perishable products are difficult to deliver; risk of customer dissatisfaction if collection times do not work for fresh goods). Shows awareness that multi-channel adds complexity as well as opportunity.
Secure (3-4 marks): At least two points on each side, linked to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One or two relevant points with limited development.
Emerging (1 mark): A single point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A national discount retailer is facing competition from a growing number of e-tailers selling similar products at lower prices.

Evaluate the extent to which switching to a multi-channel approach would be the most effective way for the retailer to remain competitive.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation identifying how a multi-channel approach could help (reaching online shoppers, offering click-and-collect, increasing brand visibility) but also recognising limits (significant investment required; discount model relies on high volume physical footfall; e-tailers have lower cost bases and may always undercut on price; brand identity may not translate online). Strong answers consider alternative strategies (price competitiveness, store experience, loyalty) and arrive at a substantiated judgement about whether multi-channel is the most important factor.
Secure (5-6 marks): At least two points for and two against, some applied to the scenario, with an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points largely one-sided or poorly applied.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points with little development and no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes 'footfall' in a retail context?
A) The number of products a store sells in a day
B) The number of people passing a retail location over a given period
C) The cost of renting a retail unit
D) The range of products available in a store
practice_questions.marks: B) The number of people passing a retail location over a given period [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two characteristics of an out-of-town retail park that would attract a large furniture retailer.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: ample parking / lower rent per square metre / large store space / access to major road networks / ability to accommodate bulky deliveries and collections / lower competition than town centre. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how locating near complementary shops can benefit a retail business.
practice_questions.marks: A simple point scores 1 mark (e.g. 'it can increase footfall'). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. 'complementary shops attract customers with similar interests — a shoe shop next to a clothing retailer draws fashion-conscious shoppers who may visit both stores in one trip'). A further developed point or second distinct mechanism scores 3 marks (e.g. add 'this is sometimes called agglomeration — the combined draw of related shops generates more total footfall than each would produce alone, increasing the chance of passing trade for every business in the cluster'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how the growth of online retailing has changed the way retail businesses think about location.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks for explaining reduced importance of high-footfall physical sites: online retailers can sell nationally without any high-street presence; their 'location' is their website and search-engine visibility; entry costs are lower because there is no property lease. Up to 2 marks for explaining new location demands created by online retailing: large, low-cost warehouses near major road and rail networks are needed to fulfil orders; for multi-channel retailers, physical stores must double as convenient click-and-collect points rather than relying purely on footfall. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A new independent coffee shop is choosing between two locations: a town-centre unit with high footfall but high rent, and a unit on an out-of-town retail park with lower rent but fewer passing pedestrians.

Discuss which location would be more suitable for the coffee shop.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5-6 marks): Balanced discussion addressing at least two factors on each side, applied to the specific scenario. For the town centre: high footfall suits impulse purchases like coffee; pedestrians and office workers are the natural target demographic; good public transport access means customers do not need cars. Against the town centre: high rent compresses margins, which is a significant issue for a small independent business. For the retail park: lower rent reduces fixed costs; however, a coffee shop relies on passing trade and impulse buying — customers at a retail park have driven there for a specific purpose and are less likely to make an unplanned stop. Supported recommendation with reasoning. Secure (3-4 marks): Two or more relevant points with some scenario application and an attempt at a recommendation. Developing (2 marks): One or two relevant points, limited development. Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A national clothing retailer currently sells exclusively through high-street stores. It is considering moving to a multi-channel approach by adding an online store.

Evaluate the extent to which moving online would reduce the importance of physical location for this retailer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7-8 marks): Evaluates multiple points on both sides. In favour of reduced importance: online sales do not depend on footfall or passing trade; the retailer can reach customers nationwide without additional physical stores; marketing shifts from window displays and high-street visibility to digital advertising and search engine optimisation; some stores may be downsized or closed if online substitutes their sales volume. Against reduced importance: physical stores still drive brand awareness, allow customers to try clothing before buying and handle returns easily — this is particularly important for fashion where fit matters; click-and-collect requires strategically located stores that are convenient for local customers; some customer demographics (older shoppers, those without internet access) still rely entirely on physical stores; the retailer's reputation and brand image is still strongly associated with its store environment. Substantiated judgement — moving online reduces but does not eliminate the importance of physical location; the nature of the product (fashion — trying on required) means stores remain a critical channel even as online sales grow. Secure (5-6 marks): At least two points on each side, some scenario application, an attempt at a judgement. Developing (3-4 marks): Mostly one-sided with limited analysis. Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points, no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following ownership types has unlimited liability?
A) Private limited company
B) Franchise
C) Sole trader
D) Public limited company
practice_questions.marks: C) Sole trader [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two ways in which the scale of a retail business affects how it operates.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct answers, for example: larger businesses have greater purchasing power to negotiate lower prices from suppliers / larger businesses can invest more in technology such as e-commerce platforms or self-serve checkouts / larger businesses have access to a wider range of finance options including issuing shares / smaller businesses have more limited promotional budgets / smaller businesses rely on personal service rather than large marketing campaigns. Do not credit the same idea twice. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by 'limited liability' and why it is an advantage for a retailer choosing to set up as a private limited company.
practice_questions.marks: Definition (1 mark): limited liability means the owner can only lose the money they invested in the business (their shares) and their personal assets are protected. Link to retailer (up to 2 marks): if the business runs into debt or fails, creditors cannot claim the owner's personal possessions such as their home or savings (1 mark); this reduces the personal financial risk of setting up and running a retail business, making entrepreneurs more willing to invest and take on the risks associated with retailing (1 mark). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of a sole trader as a form of ownership for a small independent retailer.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages (up to 2 marks): easy and inexpensive to set up with minimal paperwork (1 mark); the owner keeps all the profits and has complete control over all business decisions (1 mark); flexible working arrangements (1 mark) — max 2 marks on advantages.
Disadvantages (up to 2 marks): unlimited liability means personal assets are at risk if the business cannot pay its debts (1 mark); limited access to finance as the business cannot sell shares, restricting growth (1 mark); the owner must manage all aspects of the business alone, which can be demanding (1 mark) — max 2 marks on disadvantages. [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A couple who currently run a small independent clothing boutique as a partnership want to expand by opening three more outlets across the region. They are concerned about their personal financial risk.

Discuss whether they should convert to a private limited company (Ltd).
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion applying both sides to the scenario. For: converting to an Ltd gives limited liability, protecting their personal assets as they take on more risk with expansion; it allows them to raise additional capital by selling shares to investors, which is necessary to fund three new outlets; it improves credibility with banks and suppliers. Against: setting up an Ltd involves more complex paperwork and legal requirements; annual accounts must be filed publicly at Companies House; any shareholders brought in will share decision-making and profits; the ongoing compliance costs are higher than a partnership. A well-reasoned recommendation rounds off the answer.
Secure (3-4 marks): At least two relevant points applied to the scenario, both sides touched on.
Developing (2 marks): Points are relevant but limited in development or application.
Emerging (1 mark): A single basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A school leaver is considering buying a franchise to open a well-known sandwich shop in a busy shopping centre.

Evaluate whether a franchise is a better choice than starting an independent retail business from scratch.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation comparing franchise vs independent start-up across multiple factors. Franchise advantages: established brand reduces the time needed to build customer awareness; proven business model and training lower the risk of failure; franchisor marketing support means less promotional spend from the franchisee. Franchise disadvantages: upfront franchise fee and ongoing royalties reduce profit margins; the franchisee has little freedom to adapt the offer to local preferences; the brand's wider reputation is outside the franchisee's control. Independent advantages: full control, no royalties, ability to adapt quickly. Independent disadvantages: building brand recognition from zero takes time and investment, and the failure rate is higher. Substantiated judgement: for a school leaver with limited experience, the franchise model likely offers a safer entry into retail because the structure and support reduce risk — but this comes at a cost to long-term profitability and autonomy. The judgement is clearly supported by the evidence in the response.
Secure (5-6 marks): Both sides covered, some application to scenario, attempted judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Mostly one-sided or lacking developed application.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points, no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the correct formula for percentage change?
A) (New value ÷ Original value) × 100
B) ((New value − Original value) ÷ Original value) × 100
C) ((Original value − New value) ÷ New value) × 100
D) (New value − Original value) × 100
practice_questions.marks: B) ((New value − Original value) ÷ Original value) × 100 [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A clothing retailer sells 80 coats out of a total stock of 320 items. Calculate the percentage of stock that are coats. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: Method: (80 ÷ 320) × 100 [1 mark]. Answer: 25% [1 mark]. Accept full marks for correct answer with working shown. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: A sports shop buys a pair of trainers for £40 and sells them for £60. Calculate the mark-up percentage. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: Formula stated or implied: ((Selling price − Cost price) ÷ Cost price) × 100 [1 mark]. Correct substitution: ((60 − 40) ÷ 40) × 100 = (20 ÷ 40) × 100 [1 mark]. Correct answer: 50% [1 mark]. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A convenience store had weekly sales of £6,000 in January and £7,500 in February.

a) Calculate the percentage change in sales between January and February. [2 marks]
b) Explain what this percentage change tells the store manager about business performance. [2 marks]
practice_questions.marks: a) Percentage change = ((7,500 − 6,000) ÷ 6,000) × 100 = (1,500 ÷ 6,000) × 100 = 25% increase [2 marks: 1 for correct method, 1 for correct answer]. b) The 25% increase shows sales grew significantly between the two months (1 mark); this positive trend suggests the store may be attracting more customers or that customers are spending more per visit, so the manager could plan to maintain or increase stock levels (1 mark). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A gift shop records the following daily sales figures for one week: £320, £410, £280, £410, £390, £350, £410.

Calculate the mean, median and mode for this data. Show your working clearly.
practice_questions.marks: Mean: (320 + 410 + 280 + 410 + 390 + 350 + 410) ÷ 7 = 2,570 ÷ 7 = £367.14 (accept £367) [2 marks: 1 correct sum, 1 correct division]. Median: ordered data = 280, 320, 350, 390, 410, 410, 410; middle value (4th) = £390 [2 marks: 1 for ordering, 1 for correct answer]. Mode: £410 (appears 3 times) [2 marks: 1 for identification, 1 for correct value]. [6 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A fashion retailer generates £24,000 revenue in a month. Total costs are £18,000. On average 3,000 customers visit the store each month and 600 of them make a purchase.

Using the data above:
a) Calculate the profit for the month. [1 mark]
b) Calculate the percentage profit margin. [2 marks]
c) Calculate the conversion rate. [2 marks]
d) Analyse what these figures suggest about the retailer’s performance and identify one action the manager could take to improve results. [3 marks]
practice_questions.marks: a) Profit = 24,000 − 18,000 = £6,000 [1 mark]. b) Percentage profit margin = (6,000 ÷ 24,000) × 100 = 25% [2 marks: 1 method, 1 answer]. c) Conversion rate = (600 ÷ 3,000) × 100 = 20% [2 marks: 1 method, 1 answer]. d) Mastering (3 marks): Identifies that a 25% profit margin is a reasonable return but there is potential to improve; the 20% conversion rate means 80% of visitors leave without buying, suggesting issues with pricing, product range or customer service (2 marks); one specific, developed action recommended e.g. train staff in active selling or introduce a promotional offer to encourage impulse purchases (1 mark). Secure (2 marks): Two figures interpreted and one action suggested, but development limited. Developing (1 mark): One observation made. [8 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an economic factor that affects retail businesses?
A) The age structure of the population
B) The availability of Wi-Fi access in stores
C) The rate of inflation in the economy
D) The sourcing of ethical materials
practice_questions.marks: C) The rate of inflation in the economy [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two ways in which Christmas seasonality affects the operations of a clothing retailer.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct points, for example: increase stock levels of gift-suitable items / hire additional temporary staff / introduce seasonal promotions and window displays / extend opening hours / prepare Christmas gift packaging options. Answers that repeat the same idea score only 1 mark. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how rising interest rates could negatively affect a furniture retailer.
practice_questions.marks: A simple point scores 1 mark (e.g. "higher interest rates reduce consumer spending"). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. "consumers with mortgages have less disposable income, so they delay expensive furniture purchases, reducing the retailer's sales revenue"). A further developed point or second mechanism scores 3 marks (e.g. add "the retailer's own borrowing costs also increase if it has a business loan, squeezing profit margins at the same time as sales fall"). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how a supermarket could plan for the back-to-school seasonal peak, giving examples of the actions it might take.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 2 marks for stock planning: order increased quantities of stationery, lunchboxes, school uniform items and technology accessories well in advance of August (2 marks for a developed description with examples; 1 mark for a basic statement about ordering more stock).
Up to 2 marks for a second planning area: for example, hire additional temporary staff to manage higher footfall and restock shelves quickly; create a dedicated back-to-school aisle with promotional pricing and signage to attract parents (2 marks for a developed point with a specific example; 1 mark for a vague reference to promotions or staffing). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A city-centre fashion retailer has noticed that its sales have fallen significantly over the past year. The national unemployment rate has risen, consumer confidence is low and a rival online retailer has launched a heavily discounted app-based shopping service.

Discuss how external factors have contributed to this retailer's falling sales.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least two external factor categories with developed explanation and clear reference to the scenario. For example: high unemployment reduces consumer disposable income, so fewer people are making non-essential fashion purchases; low consumer confidence compounds this — even employed consumers may cut back on discretionary spending when they feel uncertain about the future. The technological factor is also significant: the rival's app-based discounting means consumers who do shop for fashion are more likely to buy online at a lower price than visit the city-centre store, directly reducing footfall and sales. A strong answer notes that the factors interact — economic pressure drives consumers online where they are more price-sensitive, making the technological threat more damaging.
Secure (3-4 marks): At least two factors identified and explained with some reference to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One factor identified with limited explanation.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A garden centre is planning for the coming year. It currently holds the same number of staff and the same stock levels throughout the year and does not run seasonal promotions.

Evaluate the extent to which better seasonal planning would improve the profitability of this garden centre.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation identifying specific benefits of seasonal planning (increasing stock of plants, compost, garden furniture and barbecue products in spring and summer to meet peak demand; hiring temporary staff to manage higher footfall; running spring promotions to drive early-season sales) and quantified or reasoned benefits (avoiding out-of-stock situations that lose sales to rivals; reducing January deadstock). Counter-argument engages with limitations (seasonal hiring costs money and takes time to train; over-ordering seasonal stock that sells poorly if the summer is cold can reduce profit; promotional discounting cuts margins). Substantiated judgement — e.g. seasonal planning would significantly improve profitability because the garden centre's demand is highly predictable, but the benefit depends on accurate demand forecasting and controlled buying.
Secure (5-6 marks): Clear points on both sides of the argument, some applied to the scenario, an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points largely one-sided or with a weak judgement.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points with little development and no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A retailer's monthly sales revenue figures are: January £42,000; February £38,000; March £44,000; April £39,000. Which one of the following best describes the overall trend?
A) A clear upward trend
B) A clear downward trend
C) A fluctuating but broadly flat trend
D) A strong seasonal pattern peaking in spring
practice_questions.marks: C) A fluctuating but broadly flat trend [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two features a student should look for when interpreting retail business data.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: trends / patterns / anomalies / comparing time periods / comparing stores or branches / identifying highest/lowest values / identifying percentage changes. Answers must be distinct to score 2 marks. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: A sports clothing retailer records footfall of 8,500 in October, 14,200 in November and 18,900 in December, dropping to 6,100 in January. Explain what this data tells you about the retailer's footfall pattern.
practice_questions.marks: A simple identification scores 1 mark (e.g. "footfall rises before Christmas"). A developed explanation referencing specific figures scores 2 marks (e.g. "footfall increases sharply in November and December, peaking at 18,900, which is a seasonal pattern linked to Christmas shopping"). A full explanation identifying the January anomaly or drop and offering a reason scores 3 marks (e.g. add "footfall then falls to 6,100 in January, well below October levels, likely because consumer spending drops sharply after the festive period and customers are returning gifts rather than making new purchases"). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Store A has average weekly footfall of 5,600 and weekly sales revenue of £22,400. Store B has average weekly footfall of 5,600 and weekly sales revenue of £14,000.

Describe what this data tells you about the two stores' performance and suggest one reason for the difference.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): both stores attract the same number of customers (5,600), but Store A generates 60% more revenue per week (£22,400 vs £14,000). This means Store A earns more revenue from each visitor (2 marks for a developed, data-referenced comparison; 1 mark for noting the revenue difference without development).
Reason (up to 2 marks): possible reasons include Store A selling higher-value or premium products, better-trained staff who upsell effectively, more effective visual merchandising encouraging impulse purchases, or a more affluent local customer base with higher disposable income (2 marks for a developed reason linked to the data; 1 mark for a vague suggestion). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A convenience retailer's data shows that profit has fallen from £92,000 to £68,000 over twelve months. Customer survey results show that the most common complaint is "products out of stock." Staff turnover has also increased by 30% in the same period.

Using the data provided, discuss the issues facing this retailer and recommend one solution.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Identifies and discusses multiple issues using both quantitative data (profit down by £24,000 / 26%; staff turnover up 30%) and qualitative data (out-of-stock complaints). Links the issues together logically (high staff turnover may be causing poor stock management, leading to out-of-stock situations that reduce customer satisfaction and drive down revenue and profit). Makes a clear, data-justified recommendation such as investing in staff training and retention incentives (e.g. improved pay or conditions) to reduce turnover, improve stock management and rebuild customer confidence. Justification references the data.
Secure (3-4 marks): Identifies at least two issues with some data reference and makes a relevant recommendation.
Developing (2 marks): Identifies one or two issues but with limited data reference or a vague recommendation.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A national fashion retailer has shared the following data with its management team: online sales have grown by 35% year on year; in-store sales have declined by 18% over the same period; average in-store transaction value is £62 compared with £38 online; and customer satisfaction scores for in-store shopping are higher than for online shopping.

Evaluate which retail channel the business should prioritise for investment, using the data provided to justify your recommendation.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation using all four data points. Online: 35% growth and the shift in customer behaviour are compelling reasons to invest; however, the lower average transaction value (£38 vs £62) means each online sale generates less revenue, and higher satisfaction scores in-store suggest the physical experience is more valued by customers. In-store: despite declining sales (−18%), the higher transaction value and satisfaction scores suggest investing in the store experience (e.g. improved visual merchandising, staff training, loyalty schemes) could reverse the decline and generate more revenue per customer. Substantiated judgement: e.g. the business should adopt a multi-channel strategy, investing in both channels proportionally, because relying solely on online growth risks sacrificing the higher-value in-store sales; or a clear justified choice of one channel with counter-argument acknowledged.
Secure (5-6 marks): Both sides considered with some data reference; a judgement is made but not fully justified.
Developing (3-4 marks): Mostly one-sided with limited data use.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points, little or no data used. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the aim of profit maximisation?
A) Covering all costs so the business does not make a loss
B) Earning the highest possible profit by increasing revenue or cutting costs
C) Increasing the business's share of total retail sales in its sector
D) Expanding into new products or markets to spread risk
practice_questions.marks: B) Earning the highest possible profit by increasing revenue or cutting costs [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two aims that a retail business might have beyond making a profit.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct non-financial aims, e.g.: customer satisfaction / to be ethical / environmental awareness / social responsibility / to increase market share / diversification / retail-specific aims (multi-channel, self-serve checkouts, click and collect). Answers that name the same aim in different words score only 1 mark. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a newly opened independent bakery is most likely to have survival as its main aim.
practice_questions.marks: A simple point scores 1 mark (e.g. "it needs to cover its costs"). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. "a new business has not yet built a customer base and may have high set-up costs, so its priority is generating enough revenue to pay rent, wages and stock without making a loss"). A further developed point or a distinct reason scores 3 marks (e.g. add "until the business breaks even it cannot invest in growth or brand building, so survival must come first"). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how the aims of a local independent grocery store are likely to differ from those of a large national supermarket chain.
practice_questions.marks: Independent (up to 2 marks): likely aims include survival/break-even, building a loyal local customer base, personal customer service, and community/social responsibility (2 marks for two distinct points clearly applied to the independent context; 1 mark for one point). National chain (up to 2 marks): likely aims include profit maximisation, increasing market share, expanding multi-channel operations, and building brand reputation at scale (2 marks for two distinct points clearly applied to the chain context; 1 mark for one point). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A national clothing retailer has announced it will switch all packaging to recycled materials, partner with a Fairtrade supplier for its cotton range, and donate 1% of annual profits to community projects.

Discuss the benefits and potential drawbacks of a retail business pursuing social, ethical and environmental aims.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion covering benefits (enhanced brand reputation attracts ethically conscious consumers; competitive advantage in a market where customers increasingly value sustainability; potential for media coverage and word-of-mouth marketing; staff motivation and retention) and drawbacks (ethical sourcing may increase costs, squeezing profit margins; recycled packaging may be less durable or more expensive; investing in community projects reduces funds available for growth). Scenario evidence used. Mastering answers note that benefits and drawbacks interact — e.g. short-term cost increases may be offset by long-term customer loyalty and repeat purchase.
Secure (3-4 marks): At least two points on each side with some scenario reference.
Developing (2 marks): One or two points, largely one-sided.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point, no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A sports equipment retailer has been trading for ten years. It began as a single shop focusing on survival, but now operates 60 stores nationally. The board wants to grow its share of the UK sports retail market from 8% to 15% over the next five years, while also committing to carbon-neutral delivery by 2028.

Evaluate the extent to which increasing market share should be the retailer's primary aim at this stage of its development.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation identifying why market share is a logical primary aim for a scaled, stable business (shareholders expect growth; 60 stores gives the buying power and logistics to compete aggressively; moving from 8% to 15% would significantly strengthen supplier negotiating power and reduce unit costs). Counter-argument considers competing priorities: carbon-neutral delivery will require substantial investment, potentially conflicting with profit maximisation; rapid market share growth through price competition could damage margins and threaten the very survival the business worked hard to achieve. A substantiated judgement — e.g. market share growth is appropriate but must be pursued alongside financial discipline and the environmental commitment, as neglecting either could undermine the other.
Secure (5-6 marks): At least two points on each side, some applied to the scenario, an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points but largely one-sided.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points, little development, no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the correct order for the retail supply chain?
A) Consumer → retailer → wholesaler → manufacturer
B) Manufacturer → wholesaler → retailer → consumer
C) Retailer → manufacturer → consumer → wholesaler
D) Wholesaler → consumer → retailer → manufacturer
practice_questions.marks: B) Manufacturer → wholesaler → retailer → consumer [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two factors a retailer should consider when sourcing products from a supplier.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct answers from: cost / quality / delivery time / reliability of supplier / ethical factors / environmental factors. Answers that name the same idea twice score only 1 mark. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how the human resources functional area supports a retail business.
practice_questions.marks: A simple point scores 1 mark (e.g. 'HR recruits staff'). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. 'HR recruits and trains staff, which means employees have the product knowledge and customer service skills needed to help shoppers'). A further developed explanation or second distinct HR activity scores 3 marks (e.g. additionally 'HR manages rotas and disciplinary processes, ensuring the store is always sufficiently staffed and that conduct meets expected standards'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by stock control and give one example of a stock control activity carried out by a retailer.
practice_questions.marks: Description (up to 2 marks): stock control is the process of managing stock levels to ensure sufficient products are available for customers while avoiding over-stocking (2 marks for a clear developed description; 1 mark for a basic statement that it involves managing stock). Example (up to 2 marks): for example, a supermarket uses EPOS technology so that every time a product is scanned at the checkout the stock record is automatically updated, triggering an automated re-order when levels fall below a set threshold (2 marks for a specific applied example with a benefit identified; 1 mark for a vague example without development). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A fashion retailer is planning a summer sale campaign. The marketing department has designed a promotion offering 30% off selected lines for one week.

Discuss how two other functional areas will need to work with the marketing department to ensure the campaign is successful.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5-6 marks): A developed discussion of two functional areas with clear explanation of their role and how they interact with marketing. For example: stock and merchandising must be informed about which product lines are featured so that sufficient stock is ordered in advance and the sales floor is arranged to highlight the promoted items — if stock runs out in the first day the promotion damages customer trust. Finance must approve the budget for the campaign and for any extra stock purchased, and must monitor revenue against cost to ensure the sale still generates profit rather than a loss. A high-level answer notes interdependence between all three areas and the risk of campaign failure if communication breaks down. Secure (3-4 marks): Two functional areas identified with brief explanation of each. Developing (2 marks): One functional area with some explanation. Emerging (1 mark): A basic point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A national supermarket chain is reviewing its supply chain. It currently uses a wholesaler but is considering buying direct from manufacturers.

Evaluate whether buying direct from manufacturers would be beneficial for the supermarket.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation of arguments for and against. For: cutting out the wholesaler removes an intermediary margin, lowering the cost per unit and improving profitability or allowing lower shelf prices; the retailer has greater control over quality standards and can build direct relationships with manufacturers. Against: the supermarket must now handle all large-scale warehousing itself, which requires significant capital investment in distribution centres; the buying team needs greater expertise in managing a more complex supplier network; minimum order quantities from manufacturers may be very large, tying up cash in stock. Substantiated judgement — e.g. for a national supermarket with scale and capital this is likely beneficial overall, but a smaller regional chain may lack the resources to manage it effectively. Secure (5-6 marks): At least two arguments on each side, some applied, an attempt at a judgement. Developing (3-4 marks): Points largely one-sided or lacking application. Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points with no evaluation. [8 marks]
